newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-RBNZ seen on knife edge after c/a blowout.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-RBNZ seen on knife edge after c/a blowout.

text.p: New Zealand recorded its largest ever current account deficit on Friday, prompting a sharp sell-off in the New Zealand dollar which analysts said could compel the Reserve Bank to tighten monetary conditions.

Statistics New Zealand said the current account deficit had blown out to NZ$4.47 billion in the year to March 31, with the March quarter deficit of $723 million caused by a $532 million deterioration in the seasonally adjusted invisibles deficit.
Economists polled by Reuters had on average forecast deficits of $212.2 million for the quarter and $4.1 billion for the year.
"It's pretty bad. There's no two ways about it," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

"The current account deficit is 4.8 percent of GDP when the economy is brinking on a technical recession -- it's not the kind of dynamics that I'd like to be managing," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"It really suggests to us that monetary conditions in New Zealand should be eased quite dramatically."
New Zealand financial markets agreed, sending the currency into a tail-spin but without a correspondingly severe rise in short-term interest rates.
The Kiwi's Trade-Weighted Index fell to 65.73 from 66.03, while the 90-day bank bill yield rose 18 points to 7.47 percent.

The Monetary Conditions Index, which measures the mix of the TWI and the 90-day rate, fell to 754 -- 71 points below the RBNZ's desired level of 825 in the September quarter, and 21 points outside its stated 50-point comfort zone.

"I think if we hang around here for a while it's very likely that we will see a statement or some action from the Reserve Bank," said a debt market dealer. A reduction of the bank's cash target was a possibility, dealers said.
Koukoulas said New Zealand's economic fundamentals suggested its currency should fall even further, which would only compound the Reserve Bank's dilemma.
"With the economy being very, very weak, the currency arguably being overvalued at 67 (U.S.) cents and around about 65 on the TWI, there is probably more that the currency should do," he said.

"But of course if the RBNZ is to meet their monetary conditions index (target), it means that short term interest rates have to go up, but that's not consistent with their domestic settings, so I'd be a little concerned about the way the kiwi economy is panning out at the moment."

Asked if the RBNZ was crunching the economy into the ground with its policy, geared to achieve a core inflation rate of between zero and three percent, Koukoulas said: "It's certainly the case....They have crunched the economy pretty hard. The pace of demand is very, very weak, now we have the current account problem coming through from arguably an overvalued currency."

Bankers Trust economist Nick Bennenbroek said although the New Zealand economy was expected to start rebounding in the second half of 1997, "generally when you see growth picking up it tends to put pressure on the current account as well".
"We still expect to see the current account improve, given that the currency is starting to go down and growth is reasonably subdued," he said.
"(But) it doesn't help the growth outlook if you are already at a high level (of deficit) before growth starts picking up."
